papers.title: VIPBench: A Human-Aligned Benchmark for Voice Identity Perception in the Age of Voice Cloning
papers.abstract: Speaker-recognition benchmarks test how accurately a model recovers the speaker label of a recording, treating voice identity as a property of the person who produced it. However, these benchmarks do not evaluate how humans perceive voice identity. Whether a listener hears two voices as the same person has consequences for intellectual property rights, cybersecurity, and everyday life. We introduce the Voice Identity Perception benchmark (VIPBench), which contains 124,876 same-or-different judgments from 1,290 listeners on 9,800 recording pairs from 100 public figures. The pairs include real recordings, voice clones generated by a text-to-speech system, and morphs between two speakers' voices. We also define four tasks that evaluate the alignment between speaker-representation models and human identity perception. The first two tasks measure how well a model's similarity score predicts the proportion of listeners who respond "same" and the majority response. The other two measure whether a model and listeners find the same speaker pairs similar, and whether a model's relationship to listener judgments holds equally for real and synthetic recordings. We evaluate eleven publicly available speech models. Listener judgments diverge from speaker labels most often for voice clones: in 41% of responses, listeners judged a clone and a real recording of the same speaker to be different people. No model reaches the noise ceiling; the best model explains 61% of the explainable variance. Models trained with speaker labels align with listeners better than self-supervised models do, yet a model with a 12% error rate on speaker labels aligns with listeners as well as models with error rates below 2%. VIPBench enables the evaluation of speaker models against human perception on real, cloned, and morphed speech, and our results motivate training speaker models directly on listener judgments.
papers.venue: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets (poster). 30 pages, 12 figures, 22 tables. Dataset and code: https://huggingface.co/datasets/sendfuze/vipbench
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: text-to-speech, voice cloning

papers.title: Holistic Parallel Supervision for Expressive Speech to Speech Translation
papers.abstract: Expressiveness is central to speech-to-speech translation (S2ST), yet existing datasets rarely align source and target speech jointly in content, prosody, timing, and speaker identity. Consequently, current systems often rely on indirect conditioning or transfer mechanisms. To obtain this supervision, we introduce a training-data construction strategy that combines professional dubbing, which provides human-performed correspondence in content, prosody, and timing, with multilingual voice conversion to reduce speaker mismatch. We evaluate this supervision using existing expressive S2ST systems and DirectS2ST, an end-to-end method developed in this work that predicts the complete target-speech representation directly from source speech. Experiments on English-German and English-Spanish show that holistic parallel supervision improves expressive realization across all evaluated systems. DirectS2ST exhibits the largest gains in content, prosody, timing, speaker similarity, and human-rated expressiveness. To our knowledge, this work provides the first systematic investigation of holistic parallel supervision for expressive S2ST.
papers.venue: 5 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Submitted to ICASSP 2027
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: speech translation, speech-to-speech

papers.title: GraphSeal: Graph-Augmented Speech Deepfake Detection via Temporal-Spectral Artifact Propagation
papers.abstract: Current speech deepfake detectors treat each utterance as a flat sequence of frames, limiting their ability to capture long-range spectral inconsistencies that span non-adjacent regions of an audio signal. We propose \textbf{GraphSeal}, which constructs a temporal-spectral graph over short speech segments and propagates artifact cues through graph attention layers before a global readout produces the bonafide-vs-spoof decision. Each node in the graph corresponds to a fixed-length segment; edges encode temporal adjacency and spectral similarity, letting the network attend to distant frames that share suspicious spectral patterns. A multi-head graph attention mechanism weights neighboring nodes according to both learned features and edge attributes, and a hierarchical readout aggregates node representations into a single utterance-level embedding for binary classification. GraphSeal is front-end agnostic: it operates on top of any self-supervised or handcrafted feature extractor. On ASVspoof 2019~LA, ASVspoof 2021~LA, ASVspoof~5, and the In-the-Wild dataset, GraphSeal achieves equal error rates of 0.52\%, 2.41\%, 8.17\%, and 5.24\%, respectively, matching or outperforming prior methods that rely on fixed-topology graph networks or purely sequential architectures.
reasons: Evaluation, Alignment, Safety & Copyright: speech deepfake

papers.title: CLRM: Cross-Layer Relation Modeling for Audio Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: Audio deepfake detection (ADD) aims to distinguish bonafide speech from synthetic or manipulated speech. Representations from different layers of self-supervised learning (SSL) speech encoders vary in their ability to distinguish bonafide from spoofed speech. Comparing representations of the same utterance across encoder depths may reveal useful spoofing cues, yet common layer-selection and aggregation methods do not provide these comparisons as detection inputs. We propose Cross-Layer Relation Modeling (\ours{}), which explicitly encodes cross-layer relations alongside layer-specific features, making both directly available for ADD. CLRM reuses the existing detector's SSL encoder and identifies informative layer pairs by combining speaker-relative representation geometry with source-domain detection performance. The resulting relation score is fused with the detector's original score, requiring only the training of compact relation heads and fusion parameters while keeping the existing detector frozen. Across five external datasets, CLRM reduces the mean equal error rate (EER) for all three evaluated detectors, achieving relative reductions of 7.8--16.7%. Controlled comparisons with identical layer summaries and approximately matched auxiliary-head parameter counts also show a lower mean EER for explicit relations than direct concatenation, both before and after score fusion. These findings support explicit cross-layer comparisons as useful detection inputs for SSL-based audio deepfake detectors.
reasons: Evaluation, Alignment, Safety & Copyright: audio deepfake

papers.title: Ruby-OPD: Enhancing Pronunciation Controllability and Accuracy for Flow-Matching Text-to-Speech via On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Achieving both high pronunciation accuracy and fine-grained controllability remains a central challenge in Japanese text-to-speech (TTS), as Japanese is an unsegmented language mixing logographic Kanji and phonographic Kana with extensive polyphony. Traditional cascaded systems convert text into phoneme sequences via a front-end, ensuring pronunciation control but discarding lexical semantics and prosodic cues in surface orthography. Conversely, recent zero-shot TTS models directly consume raw orthographic text to improve naturalness, yet suffer from polyphone errors and lack explicit pronunciation control. To bridge this gap, we propose a two-stage framework for flow-matching TTS. First, we investigate Ruby text representations with orthography perturbation to jointly preserve surface forms and target pronunciations for reliable control. Second, we introduce On-Policy Distillation (OPD) on large-scale text-only corpora to enhance pronunciation accuracy on raw orthographic text without paired speech. On the Joyo-Kanji-Yomi benchmark, our model achieves 97.13% Accuracy, 2.02% Target PER, 0.70% Sentence PER, and 4.21% Sentence CER under raw text while retaining strong controllability.

papers.title: LiveFoley: Dynamic Real-Time Video-to-Audio Generation for Immersive Interactive Worlds
papers.abstract: Streaming video-to-audio (V2A) generation is essential for immersive interactive applications. However, real-time constraints leave existing streaming V2A methods far behind offline models: (1) visual frontends shrink their receptive fields to cut look-ahead latency, severely degrading audio-visual alignment; (2) causal autoregressive diffusion backends denoise each audio patch in isolation, impairing audio quality. To this end, we present LiveFoley, a streaming causal autoregressive diffusion architecture that addresses both bottlenecks with imperceptible latency. For the visual frontend, we introduce a Trailing Sliding Window that converts non-causal segment-level encoders into streaming modules without retraining. By simply realigning the window, it preserves precise audio-visual alignment, while a configurable hop size reduces the frontend look-ahead well below the human perceptual threshold. Building on this tunable hop size, we propose the Unified Varhop Framework to accommodate scenarios with diverse latency and computation budgets. For the audio backend, we explore widening the denoising window of the local diffusion transformer (LocDiT) head in two temporal directions. History LocDiT adds past context to improve quality at no latency cost and serves as our default. Alternatively, Future-Warmup LocDiT breaks the autoregressive deadlock with an approximate future condition, further improving generation quality at the cost of an acceptable backend look-ahead. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LiveFoley matches offline models in temporal alignment and leads streaming systems in generation quality. Project page: https://dalision.github.io/livefoley-page/

papers.title: A Study of Artificial Intelligence-Based Emotional Music Generation Systems
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence-based affective music generation (AI-AMG) systems generate music automatically with the purpose of expressing or evoking particular feelings. This review examines studies published between 1990 and 2022 and organizes existing systems according to their main components and generation methods. A typical AI-AMG system includes target emotion identification, emotional music generation, and emotional evaluation. Rule-based, data-driven, optimization-based, and hybrid are the four categories of generation methodologies. Rule-based systems include connections between musical features and emotions, whereas data-driven systems identify structural patterns using Markov models or neural networks. Optimization methods use techniques such as genetic algorithms and graph or tree traversal, and hybrid systems combine multiple approaches. Evaluation is commonly performed through computational measures or human listener studies that assess perceived or induced emotion. Current systems can produce music associated with target emotional states, but important limitations remain, including dependence on labeled datasets, inconsistent evaluation procedures, limited measurement of induced emotion, and lower creativity than human composition. The review highlights the need for more reliable evaluation, improved emotional control, and systems that generate natural, diverse, and context-sensitive music.

papers.title: CAST-Bench: Tracing Every Sound to Its Source in Multi-Shot Audio-Video Generation
papers.abstract: Existing benchmarks for joint text-to-audio-video (T2AV) generation evaluate perceptual quality and audiovisual alignment, but balanced sound-source sam?pling and separate reporting by shot structure remain limited. This makes it dif?ficult to determine whether a specific sound is missing, attributed to the wrong source, or lost across shot transitions. To address this, we introduce CAST?BENCH, a benchmark designed to trace every generated sound back to its in?tended source in multi-shot audio-video generation. The core idea is to formu?late T2AV correctness as an audiovisual contract in which each requested sound must be emitted by the right source, synchronized with the corresponding visual action, and carry the right semantic content. Concretely, the benchmark orga?nizes 900 prompts into 9 sound-source categories, with 100 prompts per cate?gory, spanning speech, animals, instruments, ambient sounds, and other emitter types. The prompts include 439 single-shot and 461 multi-shot narratives, each derived from a structured specification that links every audio event to its emit?ter, subject, and temporal slot. The benchmark provides an 18-metric evaluation suite covering three dimensions: Visual Performance, Content Consistency, and Audio & Semantic Alignment. We further benchmark 12 representative gen?erators and find that visual quality is nearly saturated across leading systems, yet audio semantic scores still differ markedly. Across the nine shared mod?els, multi-shot prompts receive lower aggregate scores under the subset-specific scoring rules and yield different model rankings. Multi-person speech, con?sistent speaker identity across shots, and cross-shot event retention remain the main unresolved challenges. All prompts and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/yucong-liu/CAST-Bench-public.

papers.title: CRESiST: Self-Enhancing Explorative Policy Learning for Simultaneous Speech Translation
papers.abstract: Simultaneous Speech Translation (SimulST) requires balancing translation quality and latency. While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in offline translation, current LLM-based SimulST systems predominantly rely on prefix-incremental generation. This paradigm suffers from redundant Key-Value cache recomputation and necessitates external Voice Activity Detection to process unbounded streams. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose an end-to-end interleaved read-write framework built upon an omni-modal LLM. By interleaving speech chunks and text tokens, our architecture achieves full KV cache reuse, natively supporting segmentation-free, infinite-length inference. Furthermore, to learn optimal streaming policies without rigid offline alignments, we introduce a novel Actor-Critic self-enhancement pipeline. An RNN-T Actor dynamically samples read-write trajectories, while an LLM-based Critic evaluates these paths via intrinsic semantic and latency rewards, distilling the optimal policy back to the Actor. Extensive experiments on sentence-level (FLEURS, CoVoST2) and document-level (MuST-C, ACL 60/60) benchmarks demonstrate that our model establishes new state-of-the-art quality-latency Pareto frontiers, substantially outperforming existing cascaded and static-alignment baselines.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: speech translation

papers.title: Generative AI-driven high-naturalness Chinese speech synthesis model
papers.abstract: In order to solve the problems of insufficient tone continuity, abrupt stop and continuity of long sentences and distortion of spectral details in Chinese speech synthesis, a generative artificial intelligent-driven Chinese TTS model with high naturalness was constructed. The model takes the front end of the text as the input basis, maps phoneme, tone and prosodic boundaries into a unified latent space, and completes semantic-prosodic joint coding by Transformer. At the acoustic end, the conditional diffusion network is used to learn the noise addition and reverse denoising process of Mel spectrum, and the neural vocoder completes the waveform reconstruction. Experiments were conducted on 12000 Mandarin text-speech samples. The results show that the MCD of the proposed model is reduced to 4.51, F0-RMSE is 22.6, and RTF is 0.034, which is better than Tacotron2, FastSpeech2 and VITS in terms of spectrum restoration and tone stability. The validity of the model is verified.
papers.venue: International Conference on Wireless, Optical Communication, and Information Engineering (WOCIE 2026)
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: speech synthesis

papers.title: LibriSpeech-Real-QA: A Benchmark for Streaming Question Answering
papers.abstract: Most speech large language models (SLMs) still process speech in an offline manner. They only start responding after they receive the complete speech segment. However, many real-world applications require streaming speech interaction, for which the audio continuously flows in and the machine is required to answer questions based on the so far received audio chunks. For example, a user may ask the system to continuously count how many times a person's name has been mentioned while they are speaking. We observe a lack of benchmarks and evaluation protocols for real-time speech interaction. Motivated by this, we propose LibriSpeech-Real-QA, a dataset and a benchmark for real-time speech interaction. We construct different types of real-time question-answer pairs from LibriSpeech to evaluate whether speech LLMs can identify target words in streaming audio. We evaluate several popular real-time commercial models and find that they still tend to respond only after the speech turn has finished. We demonstrate that we can enable a pretrained SLM to perform this task, where we explore several modeling designs and establish a solid baseline for future research.
papers.venue: 5 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables. Submitted to IEEE ICASSP 2027
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: speech llm

papers.title: Personalized Visual Support After Automatic Speech Recognition
papers.abstract: Many spoken-language interfaces stop at producing a transcript. This project examines how a second layer of optional text and pictorial support can be adapted to individual needs. We specify four presentation levels and a behavior-based selection policy driven by replay requests, response latency and recent comprehension. After expert review of the mappings, we will compare fixed and adaptive presentation using counterbalanced spoken instructions. The study is designed to measure comprehension, usability and which modality listeners rely on, not to claim that transcript embellishment uniformly benefits listeners.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: automatic speech recognition

--- language: - en license: apache-2.0 base_model: FunAudioLLM/Fun-Audio-Chat-8B pipeline_tag: audio-to-audio tags: - full-duplex - speech-to-speech - spoken-dialogue - audio-language-model --- # Awaken Full Duplex
**Awaken: An Efficient Training Recipe for Full-Duplex Conversation That Retains Model Ability** [![Blog](https://img.shields.io/badge/Blog-Project%20Page-orange)](https://github.com/OpenmartAI/awake-audio-chat/blob/main/webpage/index.html) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Code-blue)](https://github.com/OpenmartAI/awake-audio-chat) [![Hugging Face](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97-Model-yellow)](https://huggingface.co/openmartdev/awaken-full-duplex) [![Base model](https://img.shields.io/badge/Base-Fun--Audio--Chat--8B-green)](https://huggingface.co/FunAudioLLM/Fun-Audio-Chat-8B)
## Model Description Full-duplex voice models can listen and speak at the same time, so they can acknowledge, interrupt, and hand over turns the way people do. Teaching this usually depends on natural conversational audio rich in backchannels. That audio is scarce, and without careful curation it can weaken a model's reasoning and grounding. **Awaken** learns full-duplex behavior from a small amount of such data and keeps its base model's scores.

### Key Features - **Efficient**: Starts from the half-duplex [Fun-Audio-Chat-8B](https://huggingface.co/FunAudioLLM/Fun-Audio-Chat-8B) checkpoint and teaches turn-taking with composed conversations that have explicit timing, overlap, and interruptions. Two supervised stages and a short reinforcement-learning stage are enough; there is no large-scale duplex pretraining. - **Effective**: A targeted GRPO stage raises the backchannel pass rate from 1% (supervised training alone) to **63%**, while taking the floor in only **3%** of items. - **Retains model ability**: Passes **61%** of groundedness probes, near its half-duplex base (66%) and well above open full-duplex models (14–35%). Solves **90%** of spoken logic puzzles, compared with 30–40% for open full-duplex models.

### Training Recipe

1. **Stage 1 SFT**: learns the streaming input pattern and aligned text and speech targets on 64,000 composed conversations (windows up to 180 s). 2. **Stage 2 SFT**: blends the stage-1 weights 50/50 with the base checkpoint, then continues on 100,132 records with replay of the interaction data. 3. **GRPO**: improves backchannel timing from the model's own samples in conversational windows. See the [project page](https://github.com/OpenmartAI/awake-audio-chat/blob/main/webpage/index.html) for the full data composition and training details. ## Model Details | Attribute | Value | |-----------|-------| | Model Size | ~8B parameters | | Base Model | [Fun-Audio-Chat-8B](https://huggingface.co/FunAudioLLM/Fun-Audio-Chat-8B) (half-duplex) | | Backbone | Qwen3-8B, one position per 200 ms frame | | Input | Streaming 24 kHz user audio through a causal Whisper-style encoder (2 s attention window) | | Output | Text tokens and 5 codec tokens per frame, rendered by the CosyVoice3 flow decoder and HiFT vocoder | | Interaction | Full-duplex: no turns, no voice-activity detector | | Languages | English | | License | Apache 2.0 (same as the base model) | ## Requirements - Linux with an NVIDIA GPU (CUDA) - Python >= 3.10 - PyTorch >= 2.7 (tested with 2.8, CUDA 12.8) - TensorRT 10 ## Installation ```bash git clone https://github.com/OpenmartAI/awake-audio-chat cd awake-audio-chat # 1. torch + torchaudio for YOUR CUDA driver first (the default PyPI wheel targets the newest # CUDA and will not load on older drivers), e.g. for CUDA 12.8: pip install torch torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128 # 2. the package pip install -e . # Linux + CUDA GPU; pulls transformers, tensorrt, ... pip install -e ".[fast]" # + flash-attn (faster decode; optional) pip install -e ".[voice]" # + onnxruntime, to make voice prompts from a clip ``` ## Quick Start ### Download Models ```bash pip install huggingface-hub hf download openmartdev/awaken-full-duplex --local-dir ./pretrained_models/awaken-chat ``` The speech codec is fetched automatically from [`FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512`](https://huggingface.co/FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512) (flow, vocoder and the estimator's ONNX export only). The TensorRT engine is built once per machine on first use, which takes a few minutes. ### Inference Live server (one conversation at a time, WebSocket protocol in `awaken_chat/server/protocol.py`): ```bash awaken-server --model ./pretrained_models/awaken-chat --port 8998 [--ssl-dir certs] [--voices-dir assets/voices] ``` Offline, with a recorded user track: ```bash awaken-offline --model ./pretrained_models/awaken-chat --input user.wav --out out/ # stereo.wav, transcript.txt, tokens.pt ``` Make a voice prompt from a reference clip (3-10 s of one speaker you have the rights to): ```bash awaken-voice --clip speaker.wav --out assets/voices/speaker.pt ``` From Python: ```python from awaken_chat import load_model, Decoders, DuplexSession, system_prompt loaded = load_model("./pretrained_models/awaken-chat") # HF repo id or local directory decoders = Decoders(loaded.model) # static caches + CUDA graphs, once per process session = DuplexSession(loaded.model, decoders, loaded.prompt_ids(system_prompt("You are a tour guide."))) for features in ear_frames: # (5, 4096) per 200 ms, see models/ear.py out = session.step(features) # out.text_id, out.audio_ids, out.state ``` ## Evaluation We measure listener behavior, following the conversation, and knowledge and reasoning side by side. Awaken and Fun-Audio-Chat-8B are run by us; other rows come from the public InteractionBench results and the Fun-Audio-Chat technical report. | System | Backchannel pass ↑ | Floor-take ↓ | Groundedness probes ↑ | Logic puzzles ↑ | Llama Q. ↑ | TriviaQA ↑ | |--------|-------------------:|-------------:|----------------------:|----------------:|-----------:|-----------:| | GPT-Realtime | 10% | 5% | 67% | 100% | – | – | | Moshi | 78% | 22% | 14% | 30% | 65.67 | 18.46 | | Freeze-Omni | 0% | 39% | 35% | 40% | 74.00 | 30.08 | | PersonaPlex | 83% | 11% | 30% | 30% | – | – | | Fun-Audio-Chat-Duplex-8B | – | – | – | – | 72.33 | 29.59 | | Fun-Audio-Chat-8B (half-duplex base) | n/a | n/a | 66% | 100% | 76.2 | 48.7 | | Awaken SFT | 1% | 6% | 62% | 87% | 70.7 | 35.5 | | **Awaken GRPO** | **63%** | **3%** | **61%** | **90%** | **73.4** | **36.2** | - **Backchannels**: 30 InteractionBench storytelling items × 3 seeds. An item passes when the assistant backchannels at least once and never takes the floor. A half-duplex model cannot speak while the user is speaking, so the base model is n/a. - **Groundedness**: 10 conversations of 22–24 turns, then 52 probes (recall, updates, unknown information, constraints, false premises, nonsense questions). Our rows are means over 5–30 runs judged on the model's text stream; published rows judge transcripts of the audio. - **Logic puzzles**: 10 InteractionBench puzzles × 3 seeds, judged on the model's text stream. - **Spoken QA**: our rows are means over 3 seeds; Freeze-Omni, Moshi and Fun-Audio-Chat-Duplex-8B are reported scores from Table 7 of the Fun-Audio-Chat technical report. Because our runs and the published results are scored differently, compare across systems with care. Full methodology is on the [project page](https://github.com/OpenmartAI/awake-audio-chat/blob/main/webpage/index.html). ## Inference Details
How the inference stack works Every 200 ms ("one frame") the model consumes * the user's audio of that frame, through a causal **ear** (a Whisper-style encoder with a 2 s attention window), * its own previous frame: one **text token** and five **codec tokens** of its own voice, and predicts the next text token and the next five codec tokens. The text lane carries the words and two control tokens: `pad` means "listening" and, during speech, "I am done" (the release); `sil` means "words done, audio still finishing". The codec tokens are rendered to speech by CosyVoice3's flow-matching decoder and HiFT vocoder. ``` mic 24 kHz ─► StreamingEar ─► 5 feature vectors per frame ─┐ ▼ own text token ──► Qwen3-8B backbone (one position per frame) ──► next text token own codec tokens ─┘ │ ▼ depth decoder (5 codec tokens / frame) ──► CosyVoice3 flow + HiFT ──► speaker ``` Both transformer stacks run through a fused, CUDA-graphed single-token decoder with static key/value caches (`awaken_chat/inference/static_decoder.py`), so a frame costs a few milliseconds of launch overhead instead of thousands of small kernels.
Decode parameters `DecodeParams` (`awaken_chat/inference/params.py`) has two presets. `bench` is the recipe the reported numbers were produced with (text T 0.7 / top-k 25, audio T 0.8 / top-k 250). `live` is sharper inside a text burst (T 0.2 / top-k 5), penalizes repeated content tokens and caps consecutive near-silent codec tokens; it is what the server uses by default. Any field can be overridden per conversation in the `start` message.
Repository layout ``` awaken_chat/ frame.py frame rate, group size, sample rates, special token ids, system prompt models/ configuration, ear, token embedder, depth decoder, AwakenModel, loaders inference/ static decoder, session state machine, sampling, decode params, offline runner codec/ CosyVoice3 flow + HiFT (vendored, trimmed), streaming detokenizer, worker process, voices server/ WebSocket protocol, live session runner, FastAPI app cli.py awaken-server / awaken-offline / awaken-voice scripts/ ws_client.py, a paced WebSocket client that drives the server from a wav file tests/ CPU unit tests on tiny random models hf_model_card/ Hugging Face model card (README + figures) webpage/ project page ```

See [`NOTICE`](https://github.com/OpenmartAI/awake-audio-chat/blob/main/NOTICE). ## Contact - 🐛 Submit an [Issue](https://github.com/OpenmartAI/awake-audio-chat/issues) - 💡 Submit a [Pull Request](https://github.com/OpenmartAI/awake-audio-chat/pulls)

[![Source on GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/source-GitHub-1D1B20?logo=github)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet) [![staleynet-audio on crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/staleynet-audio?label=staleynet-audio)](https://crates.io/crates/staleynet-audio) [![Paper](https://img.shields.io/badge/paper-PDF-6750A4)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/blob/main/paper/preprint.pdf) [![Book](https://img.shields.io/badge/book-mdBook-6750A4)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/tree/main/book/src) [![Release v0.1.2](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/arpanpathak/staleynet)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/releases) [![Dataset: 3.1 GB](https://img.shields.io/badge/dataset-3.1%20GB-FFD21E?logo=huggingface&logoColor=black)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/arpanpathak/staleynet-data)

Weights for **StaleyNET**, a text-prompted music generator trained from random initialization in Rust on NVIDIA edge GPUs. The Transformer, residual vector quantizer, Griffin-Lim vocoder, and GPU kernels are implemented in the project.

The code, paper, and book live in the companion repository:
<https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet>.

## Release v0.1.2

- GitHub release: <https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/releases/tag/v0.1.2>
- `staleynet-audio` 0.1.2 on crates.io: <https://crates.io/crates/staleynet-audio>. Its page explains each audio step with intuition and runnable examples.
- Since v0.1.1: the GPU kernels are organised into one module per topic, the AGX Thor builds against cuda-oxide's main branch, and the paper has been revised with hardware, benchmark and tokenizer appendices.
- New in these repositories: the `lyrics-thor`, `lyrics-thor-long` and `pq-large` runs, and the band-group token caches they train on.
- CI: rustfmt, clippy with warnings denied, cargo-deny, the audio coverage gate, and documentation tests for every example on the crate page.

The step values are exactly what each `model.json` records. `best/` is the weight-only checkpoint selected by validation. `latest/` is the resumable checkpoint with AdamW moments. Some early runs stored only `best/`, and `thor-base` and `smoke` record step 0 in their `best/model.json`. Where a `latest/` exists, prefer it for the late training state.

### About `pq-large`

`pq-large` is still training on the Jetson AGX Thor (128 GB). The files here are a snapshot at step 7,000 of 20,000, and they will be replaced as the run advances. Its validation loss (5.135 nats per token at step 7,000) is averaged over 16 codebooks of a different tokenizer, so it cannot be compared directly with the 4-codebook runs above.

The model reads codes from the band-group tokenizer, which splits the 128 mel bands into 4 groups and quantises each group with 4 residual levels. That tokenizer is stored as `checkpoints/pq-large/tokenizer.json`, and the matching caches are `cache-g4l4f1/`, `cache-pq-jamendolyrics/` and `cache-pq-recordings/` in the dataset repository. Pass `--cache data/cache-g4l4f1` when generating with this run.

`evaluations/<run>/` holds the paired lyrics test of each lyrics run: the per-track loss with aligned, removed and mismatched lyrics.

## Training progress

The runs on the Jetson AGX Thor publish their metrics here every two hours
(`deploy/hf/publish.sh` in the code repository): `metrics/<run>.jsonl` holds
every logged event, and `plots/<run>.png` shows, from left to right, the
training and validation loss in nats per code against optimizer step, the
latest validation loss of each codebook (coarse levels are far easier to
predict than fine ones), and the throughput in positions per second.

![pq-large training curves](plots/pq-large.png)

## Layout

```text
checkpoints/<run>/best/      weights only       model.json + tensors.bin
checkpoints/<run>/latest/    weights + AdamW    model.json + tensors.bin
configs/                     canonical training configurations
run-configs/                 per-run config.json where the run saved one
metrics/                     full metrics.jsonl for every run
logs/                        captured training logs and the tokenizer sweeps
evaluations/<run>/           paired lyrics evaluations
```

`tensors.bin` is little-endian `f32` in parameter-visitor order. `latest/` appends the AdamW first moments and then the second moments. `model.json` records the tensor manifest, the step, whether optimizer state is present, and the training configuration.

## Download and use

```bash
hf download arpanpathak/staleynet-checkpoints \
  --repo-type model --local-dir staleynet-checkpoints

# From the code repository, on a Jetson with the cuda-oxide toolchain:
cargo oxide build -- --release
staleynet sing \
  --cache data/cache \
  --run staleynet-checkpoints/checkpoints/thor-base/best \
  --prompt "slow acoustic ballad, warm female voice" \
  --out song.wav
```

For the lyrics model:

```bash
staleynet sing \
  --run staleynet-checkpoints/checkpoints/lyrics-orin/best \
  --prompt "grunge rock, raw male voice" \
  --lyrics-file song.txt \
  --out song.wav
```

Architecture: width 256, 8 heads, 6 layers, feed-forward multiplier 4, context length 768, 4 residual codebooks of 1024 entries, 128 mel bands at 24 kHz. `lyrics-orin` adds a 256-byte lyrics field.

## Training data and licensing

- **Song Describer Dataset** (SDD), Zenodo record [10072001](https://zenodo.org/records/10072001): 706 Jamendo recordings with human captions. Captions are CC BY-SA 4.0. The recordings carry the per-track Creative Commons licenses in `audio_licenses.txt`, including CC BY-NC-ND and CC BY-NC-SA.
- **JamendoLyrics MultiLang**, <https://github.com/f90/jamendolyrics>: code and metadata are MIT. Songs and lyrics carry the per-song CC licenses in `JamendoLyrics.csv`.

Because the training audio includes NonCommercial and NoDerivatives tracks, these checkpoints are research artifacts, not a commercial product. Do not use them commercially where the upstream recording licenses forbid it, and do not use them to impersonate a singer without consent.

The checkpoint files are offered under CC BY-SA 4.0 (`LICENSE-CC-BY-SA-4.0.txt`) to the extent the upstream dataset licenses allow. See `NOTICE` for the full provenance statement and `SHA256SUMS` for integrity.

## Known limitations

- Griffin-Lim produces phasey audio compared with a learned vocoder.
- The models are small edge models, not production music systems.
- The lyric models were trained on a small lyrics subset, so lyric intelligibility is limited.
- The checkpoints are research artifacts and have no warranty.

# Matoub-4B

A 4B-parameter neural speech synthesis and voice cloning foundation model for **Kabyle** (Taqbaylit, `kab`, Latin script), trained on 384,960 curated speech pairs from Common Voice Kabyle. Given Kabyle text and a short reference recording with its transcript, it synthesises broadcast-quality **24 kHz audio** that reproduces the vocal timbre, prosodic contours, and acoustic presence of the target speaker.

Matoub-4B brings zero-shot, reference-conditioned voice cloning to Kabyle, supporting both native and cross-lingual cloning out of the box. A speaker recorded in English, French, Arabic, or any other supported language can speak fluent Taqbaylit with their natural vocal identity and expressive dynamics preserved. Generating speech across an 8-codebook discrete audio representation, the model faithfully captures Kabyle's rich phonology — including spirantised, pharyngealised, emphatic, and geminated consonants.

## Results

Validation was conducted across 16 utterances spanning six speakers. Speaker similarity
is evaluated using WeSpeaker 256-dimensional speaker embeddings, and transcription fidelity
is verified using Fadhma-300M ASR.

| metric | value |
|---|---|
| utterances | 16 |
| terminated | 15 / 16 |
| **mean voice cosine** | **0.881** |
| CER excess over real-audio floor | 0.045 |

The measured mean voice cosine of 0.881 confirms consistent speaker identity retention
across reference speakers. The CER excess measures character error rate relative to human
recordings of the same texts.

## Intended use

- **Kabyle audio production**: narration, dialogue, and spoken content.
- **Accessibility**: screen readers and voice interfaces for Kabyle speakers.
- **Language learning**: pronunciation material and spoken references.
- **Voice research**: cross-lingual speech synthesis and reference conditioning.

**Not suitable for**: biometric identification, impersonation, or safety-critical applications.

## Usage

```bash
pip install "transformers==5.17.0" "torch==2.11.0" "torchaudio==2.11.0" soundfile onnxruntime
```

Load the model with `transformers`. The custom architecture is loaded directly via
`trust_remote_code=True`:

```python
import soundfile as sf
from transformers import AutoModelForTextToWaveform

REPO = "agbalu/Matoub-4B"
model = AutoModelForTextToWaveform.from_pretrained(REPO, trust_remote_code=True).to("cuda").eval()

speech = model.generate(
    text="Azul fell-awen! Ass-a ad nemmeslay s teqbaylit.",
    reference_audio="voice.wav",
    reference_text="The exact words spoken in voice.wav, in their original language.",
)

sf.write("speech.wav", speech.waveform[0].numpy(), speech.sampling_rate, subtype="FLOAT")
```

### Notes

- `text`: target Kabyle text to synthesise.
- `reference_audio`: path to clean reference audio of the target speaker.
- Use clear, continuous speech from one speaker, without background music, overlapping voices or heavy reverberation. No single optimal reference duration has been established for this release.
- `reference_text`: exact transcript of the words spoken in `reference_audio` in their original language.
- For an English or French reference, provide the exact English or French transcript; do not translate it into Kabyle.
- The returned waveform is a CPU float tensor sampled at 24,000 Hz.
- The generation pipeline can verify candidate outputs for transcript accuracy (Fadhma-300M CER), speaker similarity (WeSpeaker cosine), and audio quality (TorchAudio SQUIM) before returning the final waveform. Longer texts are handled via automatic sentence segmentation. All inference and sampling parameters are configured in `model.config.inference`.

### Generation settings and return value

`.generate()` accepts `text`, `reference_audio`, `reference_text`, and optional
`output_path`. Sampling settings are configured before generation:

```python
model.config.inference["sampling"].update(
    temperature=0.8,
    top_p=0.8,
    top_k=30,
    max_new_positions=1500,
)
```

These are the packaged sampling defaults. `max_new_positions` limits each
candidate's generated codec positions; it is not a waveform sample count.
The return value is `SpeechOutput`:

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| `.waveform` | CPU float tensor with shape `[1, N]` |
| `.sampling_rate` | `24000` |
| `.report` | Generation audit with segment-level candidate scores, selection and verification results |

The engine evaluates CER, speaker cosine and predicted SQUIM quality when
selecting candidates. These checks can reject a request; they do not guarantee
perfect pronunciation or voice identity.

### 4-bit Quantization (NF4)

Install the additional quantization dependencies:

```bash
pip install "bitsandbytes==0.50.2" "accelerate==1.15.0"
```

For consumer GPUs and low-memory environments (e.g. RTX 3060, T4, 8 GB laptop GPUs), load the model using 4-bit NormalFloat (`nf4`). The transformer backbone is compressed while the neural vocoder automatically remains in high precision:

```python
import soundfile as sf
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForTextToWaveform, BitsAndBytesConfig

REPO = "agbalu/Matoub-4B"
bnb_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    load_in_4bit=True,
    bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)

model = AutoModelForTextToWaveform.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    quantization_config=bnb_config,
    device_map="auto",
    trust_remote_code=True,
).eval()

speech = model.generate(
    text="Azul fell-awen! Ass-a ad nemmeslay s teqbaylit.",
    reference_audio="voice.wav",
    reference_text="The exact words spoken in voice.wav, in their original language.",
)

sf.write("speech.wav", speech.waveform[0].numpy(), speech.sampling_rate, subtype="FLOAT")
```

The NF4 loading path was verified, including preservation of the audio codec in
FP32. On the measured single-candidate development panel, it reduced memory but
degraded pronunciation and completion relative to BF16. Prefer BF16 for the
Python quality baseline.

| Loading format | Measured peak device memory (decimal GB) |
|---|---:|
| BF16 | 9.94 |
| BitsAndBytes NF4 | 4.57 |

These peaks were measured on an H100 MIG using single-candidate decoding, with
quality scoring on CPU. They are not full-pipeline hardware requirements:
GPU-based verification models and longer contexts require additional memory.
Other GPU types were not benchmarked.

### Companion GGUF release

Standalone `q4_k`, `q8_0`, and `bf16` GGUF packages are prepared separately at
[`agbalu/Matoub-4B-GGUF`](https://huggingface.co/agbalu/Matoub-4B-GGUF).
See that card for runtime requirements, measurements and format-specific limits.

## Architecture

Matoub-4B couples an autoregressive multimodal transformer backbone with an 8-codebook 24 kHz neural audio codec. Parameter adaptation targets all projection pathways across every decoder layer, optimizing speech synthesis and phonetic fidelity while preserving the extensive cross-lingual acoustic representations of the foundation model.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Parameters** | **4,109,540,864** |
| Base model | bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b |
| Codec | bosonai/higgs-audio-v2-tokenizer (8 codebooks, 24 kHz) |
| Output | 24 kHz mono audio |
| Context length | Up to 8,192 positions |
| Interface | Transformers `AutoModelForTextToWaveform` (`trust_remote_code=True`) |

## Training data

Trained on Common Voice 26.0 Kabyle speech resampled to 24 kHz. Utterances are paired with
distinct same-speaker reference recordings sharing no text or audio overlap.

| split | pairs |
|---|---|
| train | 384,960 |
| validation | 29,812 |
| test | 5,871 |
| **total** | **420,643** |

## Training recipe

| | |
|---|---|
| Objective | Autoregressive cross-entropy over 8 codec streams |
| Adaptation | Rank-32 LoRA (alpha 64) |
| Optimizer | AdamW |
| Learning rate | 5e-5 with cosine decay to 5e-6 |
| Batch size | 32 |
| Precision | bfloat16 |
| Steps | 12,030 |
| Final loss | 3.8997 nats |

## Limitations

- **Pronunciation edge cases**: Proper nouns, loanwords, or atypical spellings outside the training corpus may require manual pronunciation adjustments.
- **Language specificity**: Optimized specifically for Kabyle (`kab`). Sibling Amazigh varieties (e.g. Tarifit, Tashelhit) have distinct phonological structures and are not covered.

## Files

| file | description |
|---|---|
| `model.safetensors` | Model weights with merged LoRA adaptation and audio codec |
| `config.json` | Model configuration and AutoClass mapping |
| `tokenizer.json`, `tokenizer_config.json`, `chat_template.jinja` | Text tokenizer and template |
| `modeling_speech.py` and supporting modules | Transformers model implementation |
| `requirements.txt` | Runtime dependencies |
| `export.stats.json` | Package checksums and metadata |
| `LICENSE`, `NOTICE` | Licensing terms |

## Reproduction

Trained on 384,960 Common Voice 26.0 Kabyle pairs for 12,030 steps from `bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b`. All reported metrics reproduce directly from the published weights and configuration.

## The name

**Lounès Matoub** (1956–1998) was one of the most celebrated Kabyle singers and poets of the 20th century, and an iconic advocate for Taqbaylit. Across 36 albums recorded in Kabyle, his music and poetry made the language vibrant and audible to generations of listeners.

His voice remains deeply tied to the preservation and cultural vitality of the language. Naming a Kabyle speech synthesis model after him is an homage to that legacy: using technology to make the language heard and spoken.

The naming is homage; it implies no affiliation or endorsement.

## Citation

```bibtex
@software{agbalu_matoub_4b_2026,
  title  = {Matoub-4B: Reference-Conditioned Kabyle Speech Synthesis},
  author = {AƔBALU},
  year   = {2026},
  url    = {https://huggingface.co/agbalu/Matoub-4B},
  note   = {4B-parameter neural speech synthesis foundation model for Kabyle; 24 kHz}

```

The model weights are distributed under the **Boson Higgs TTS 3 Research and Non-Commercial License**, inheriting the terms of the base model ([`bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b`](https://huggingface.co/bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b)). The weights are strictly for non-commercial research use.

The training data derives from Mozilla Common Voice Kabyle (CC0-1.0, public domain). The supporting evaluation models ([Fadhma-300M](https://huggingface.co/agbalu/Fadhma-300M), [WeSpeaker](https://huggingface.co/Wespeaker/wespeaker-voxceleb-resnet34-LM)) retain their respective licences (Apache-2.0 and CC BY 4.0).

# Matoub-4B (GGUF)

Standalone GGUF weights for [Matoub-4B](https://huggingface.co/agbalu/Matoub-4B),
a reference-conditioned Kabyle speech synthesis model producing 24 kHz mono audio.

## Provided quantizations

| File | Size (decimal GB) | Use |
|---|---:|---|
| `Matoub-4B-q4_k.gguf` | 3.912 | Recommended compact option on the measured development panel |
| `Matoub-4B-q8_0.gguf` | 5.934 | Higher-precision decoder option |
| `Matoub-4B-bf16.gguf` | 9.724 | Native runtime precision baseline |

All formats preserve **all 528 codec tensors in FP32**, with values verified
against the source. Quantization applies to eligible generator tensors. Required
configuration and tokenizers are embedded. No separate codec download is needed.

## Measurements

Measured on one H100 NVL MIG 3g.47gb, four text/reference cases and two seeds per
case. Each request used one decoding attempt, a 600-position limit, temperature
0.8, top-p 0.8 and top-k 30.

| Format | Peak device memory (GB) | RTF on completed outputs | Completed / attempted |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| BF16 | 9.904 | 0.290 | 5 / 8 |
| Q8_0 | 6.694 | 0.284 | 4 / 8 |
| Q4_K | 4.716 | 0.138 | 5 / 8 |

RTF is synthesis time divided by generated audio duration; lower is faster.
It includes reference processing and waveform decoding, excludes model loading
and quality scoring, and is weighted by successful audio duration. Failed
requests are counted separately. Different completion subsets prevent interpreting
these values as a controlled speedup ratio. Memory is a sampled peak above idle
device usage, not a minimum hardware requirement.

On the four requests completed by both Q4_K and native BF16 (280 normalized
characters), Fadhma-300M CER was 7.14% versus 8.21%; WeSpeaker cosine was 0.542
versus 0.546. Predicted SQUIM quality was 4.180 versus 4.191. This small panel
supports Q4_K as a compact option; it does not prove equivalent quality for all
speakers or texts. Q8_0 is offered for precision preference, not as a measured
quality winner. Q4_0 is excluded after weaker results.

## Usage

Use [audio.cpp](https://github.com/0xShug0/audio.cpp), verified at v0.9.4,
commit `f7ac446fb75e594a6913c846bea6c85b637f6ac0`, with CUDA on SM90.
This speech GGUF requires that runtime's `higgs_audio_tts` family; a generic
text-only GGUF loader is not sufficient. CPU and other accelerators were not
qualified in this release.

```bash
audiocpp_cli --task clon --family higgs_audio_tts \
  --model Matoub-4B-q4_k.gguf --backend cuda \
  --text "Azul fell-awen! Ass-a ad nemmeslay s teqbaylit." \
  --voice-ref voice.wav \
  --reference-text "The exact words spoken in voice.wav." \
  --max-tokens 1500 \
  --session-option higgs_audio_tts.codec_weight_type=f32 \
  --out speech.wav
```

Use a clean single-speaker reference and its exact transcript. The native runtime
has its own decoding path. It does not include the Transformers package's ASR,
speaker verification or multi-candidate selection. The example's larger limit
does not guarantee completion; generation may still repeat or reach the limit.

## Main model and limitations

See [Matoub-4B](https://huggingface.co/agbalu/Matoub-4B) for the Python interface,
intended use, pronunciation limitations and citation. Voice identity and
pronunciation vary across reference recordings. Use voices with permission and
identify synthetic speech appropriately.

## Licence

The weights follow the Boson Higgs TTS 3 Research and Non-Commercial License.
Read the included `LICENSE` and `NOTICE` before use or redistribution.

Outputs base Kokoro compatible voice packs @ `[510, 1, 256]`. ([write-up](https://remsky.art/writeups/kokoro-fastapi/inno-clone/)) ## Samples Same passage for every voice, enrolled from the references. LibriTTS-R speakers are `dev-clean` held out from training. | voice | tuned | reference | |---|---|---| | am_libritts1272 | | | | af_libritts5338 | | | | am_libritts6241 | | | | af_ameliaearhart | | | | bf_janegoodall | | | | am_vincentprice | | | ## Usage Code available on Github: [remsky/inno-kokoro](https://github.com/remsky/inno-kokoro). Integrated into [Kokoro-FastAPI](https://github.com/remsky/Kokoro-FastAPI) (v0.9.0+) ```bash pip install inno-kokoro ``` Enrolling a voice: ```python from inno_kokoro.enroll import Tuner, enroll, read from kokoro import KPipeline tuner = Tuner() # pulls model.safetensors into the huggingface cache pack, _ = enroll(*read("my_ref.wav"), tuner) pipe = KPipeline(lang_code="a") wav = next(pipe("Hello from a tuned voice.", voice=pack)).audio ``` The pack is a plain tensor; `torch.save(pack, "voices/am_me.pt")` makes it a voice file like any other, prefixed by accent and gender like the stock packs. The pitch-tracking ceiling is set automatically from the reference's harmonic spacing, so band-limited or archival sources land in the right octave without tuning. - `enroll(..., fmax=180)` overrides it if a voice still reads the wrong register. ### Architecture A 5 to 30 s reference clip in, a stock-shaped Kokoro voice pack out. Everything loads from `model.safetensors`, no extra downloads.
Architecture details Enrollment embeds an input audio sample via the baked speaker encoder and maps through `model.safetensors` to build the encoder side; prosody aspects are measured to build the predictor half. - **speaker encoder**: a 6.6M-param WeSpeaker ResNet34 distilled from [**UniSpeech-SAT-sv**](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/unispeech-sat-base-plus-sv) embeddings - matches within 0.002 speaker cosine on hold-out dev-clean (380mb fp32 -> 14mb fp16) - **style head**: the decoder (timbre) half of the pack comes from the speaker embedding (512) mapped to Kokoro style (256). Shifts along a learned spectral-tilt direction by the reference's measured tilt. - **prosody blend**: the predictor (prosody) half uses the stock Kokoro packs as a foundation: - Blended by nonnegative least squares to the reference F0 mean, F0 spread and syllable rate. - Packs more than 4 st from the reference's pitch are excluded. - Higher graded packs are weighted as preferred during selection. - **prosody head** (v0.2): a linear adjust on the blend from the reference's F0 mean and spread, - fitted to deltas optimized through the frozen predictor. `enroll(..., head=False)` skips it. Enrollment runs in about 0.05 s per second of reference on CPU (a 30 s reference in 1.4 s) and 0.1-0.3 s total on a GPU, after the one-time model load. Total model size @ fp16: ~24mb
## Limits - English trained (LibriTTS-R) currently - Some texture/identity is traded to maintain audio quality and stability within Kokoro's range. - Rythym is a best-effort match to the speaker. - Prosody is a convex blend of stock prosody by pitch, spread and pace. Outside of that range, it will only pin to the nearest edge - Reference clip requirements: - 3 second minimum, up to a max of 30s - Reasonably free of audio artifacts - Single speaker ## Training and Metrics All stages: Kokoro frozen; LibriTTS-R train-clean-100 unless noted. Trained via HF Jobs `a10g-small`; under $20 in GPU time:
v0.1.0 training notes - Stage 1: mapped speaker embedding to timbre: - Style head on a speaker-embedding cycle loss: clone, render, re-embed, cosine to the input audio embedding. - [10k steps: dev cosine ~0.92; nearest stock voice baseline 0.857] - Stage 2: the embedding alone missed texture and pitch; adjustments: - Augmented pitch and speed. Added losses via a WavLM layer-statistics L1, a small log-F0 error, and spectral-tilt. - [11k steps: dev cosine 0.934, DNSMOS 3.30] - Stage 3: tuned the encoder side to match the blended predictors: - Predictor half fixed to the blended rows, only the decoder half trained. - [3k steps: dev cosine 0.932, DNSMOS 3.48] - Stage 4: distilled the speaker encoder so enrollment needs no UniSpeech download: - WeSpeaker ResNet34 plus a projection, trained on `1 - cos(student, teacher)` over LibriTTS-R crops with synthetic channel damage; the style head is untouched. - [20k steps: hold-out dev-clean parity, DNSMOS equal; archival references sat about 0.05 behind the teacher] - Stage 5: the student lagged the teacher on archival references; synthetic damage had plateaued: - Mixed real public-domain archival broadcast audio into the distillation crops. - [8k steps: archival cosine up 0.03-0.05, DNSMOS unchanged]
v0.2.0 training notes - Stage 1: the blend under-predicted pitch range and sentence-final falls: - Fitted a predictor-half delta per speaker (426; adds VoxPopuli-en and Emilia-YODAS EN) - Targeted F0 mean, spread, IQR, pause fraction and speech time. - Ridge head from reference F0 mean + spread to the fitted delta. - [hold-out: F0 mean error 0.9 -> 0.45 st, spread 0.6 -> 0.35 st, IQR 0.9 -> 0.5 st] - Stage 2: the student trailed the teacher on public-speaking and in-the-wild references: - Added VoxPopuli and Emilia speakers to the distillation crops. - [8k steps: hold-out cosine VoxPopuli 0.976 -> 0.986, Emilia 0.964 -> 0.983; WavLM cosine 0.941 -> 0.944, DNSMOS unchanged] - Stage 3: the timbre half had only seen LibriTTS speakers: - Repeated v0.1.0 stage 3 with VoxPopuli and Emilia speakers in the draw. - [3k steps: WavLM cosine samples 0.927 -> 0.935, dev-clean 0.956 -> 0.959, VoxPopuli 0.926 -> 0.939, Emilia 0.931 -> 0.936; DNSMOS unchanged]
### Zero-shot identity benchmark Inno gets about a third of the normalized similarity range, twice as close as the nearest stock pack (with UTMOS intact and keeping Kokoro's stable natural style).
Full benchmark results and methodology LibriSpeech test-clean, F5-TTS cross-sentence split (1127 utterances, 39 held-out speakers. Reference in, new sentence out, scored against the speaker's real recording. - normalized: how far the render sits between sounding like a stranger (0) and a second real take of the speaker (1) - RTF: RTX 4060 Ti | system | SIM-o | normalized | ECAPA | UTMOS | RTF | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | ground truth (second recording) | 0.695 | 1.00 | 0.656 | 4.10 | | | F5-TTS v1 base | 0.650 | 0.94 | 0.713 | 3.86 | 0.48 | | StyleTTS2 (LibriTTS zero-shot) | 0.386 | 0.46 | 0.415 | 4.40 | 0.06 | | **Inno v0.2** | 0.288 | 0.32 | 0.288 | 4.45 | 0.07 | | OpenVoice v2 | 0.227 | 0.23 | 0.316 | 3.80 | 0.12 | | Kokoro, nearest stock pack | 0.167 | 0.15 | 0.215 | 4.25 | 0.06 | StyleTTS2 uses a related architecture with an unfrozen decoder, a possible ceiling for this style space. - StyleTTS2: alpha 0.3, beta 0.7, 5 steps. - OpenVoice v2: MeloTTS EN-US, tau 0.3. - F5-TTS: 32 NFE, CFG 2.
v0.1 vs v0.2 shipped-weight comparison Measured on the shipped weights through the stock `KPipeline`: one fixed passage rendered for the seven sample voices plus ten hold-out dev-clean speakers, F0 by Praat over 6 s chunks with the reference's tracking ceiling applied to both sides. | metric | v0.1 blend only | v0.2 with head | |---|---|---| | speaker cosine (WavLM-sv), samples / dev-clean | 0.926 / 0.956 | 0.935 / 0.959 | | F0 mean, render minus reference | 0.65 st mean abs | 0.8 st mean abs | | F0 spread, render minus reference | 0.65 st mean abs | 0.5 st mean abs | | DNSMOS | 3.50 | 3.50 | The head's gain is spread; on F0 mean it scatters more per speaker and flips the signed bias from -0.2 to +0.3 st.
## Licenses and credits Adapter weights and code: Apache-2.0, except the baked speaker encoder (`enc.*` in `model.safetensors`), which is CC BY-SA 3.0 (see below) - Built on [hexgrad/Kokoro-82M](https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/Kokoro-82M) (Apache-2.0, StyleTTS2 architecture) - The speaker encoder is a [WeSpeaker](https://github.com/wenet-e2e/wespeaker) ResNet34 (code Apache-2.0) - initialised from the [VoxCeleb-trained ResNet34-LM weights](https://huggingface.co/Wespeaker/wespeaker-voxceleb-resnet34-LM) (CC BY 4.0) - distilled from [microsoft/unispeech-sat-base-plus-sv](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/unispeech-sat-base-plus-sv) - (Microsoft UniSpeech, [CC BY-SA 3.0 on GitHub](https://github.com/microsoft/UniSpeech/blob/main/LICENSE)); encoder weights under CC BY-SA 3.0 - Training data (no audio redistributed beyond the samples): - [LibriTTS-R](https://www.openslr.org/141/) (CC BY 4.0), also the LibriTTS sample references - [VoxPopuli](https://github.com/facebookresearch/voxpopuli) (CC0) - [Emilia-YODAS](https://huggingface.co/datasets/amphion/Emilia-Dataset) EN (CC BY 4.0) - Sample references: - Amelia Earhart from ["Speech by Amelia Earhart"](https://www.loc.gov/item/afccal000004/), Library of Congress AFC 1986/022 - Jane Goodall from [BBC Woman's Hour excerpt](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Jane_Goodall_BBC_Radio4_Woman%27s_Hour_26_Jan_2010_p00tr6ks.flac), BBC, CC BY 3.0 - Vincent Price public domain from ["The House On Haunted Hill"](https://archive.org/details/The_House_On_Haunted_Hill) Only clone voices you have permission to clone, even the shallow cloning offered via this model and technique.

# XTTS-v2 Romanian

> **A newer version is available: [XTTS-v2 Romanian v2](https://huggingface.co/eduardem/xtts-v2-romanian-v2)** — 15 voices, ~470 speakers, ~471K training clips. Trained on a combined dataset 3x larger than v1.

Fine-tuned [XTTS-v2](https://huggingface.co/coqui/XTTS-v2) for high-quality Romanian text-to-speech with voice cloning. Achieves **6.3% WER** (measured by Whisper large-v3) across 5 distinct voices trained on ~150 hours of Romanian speech.

**[Live Demo & Audio Samples](https://eduardm.codeberg.page/romanian-tts-xtts-v2/)** | **[Training Code (Codeberg)](https://codeberg.org/eduardm/romanian-tts-xtts-v2)**

## Audio Samples

### Costel (male, literary narration) — 1.9% WER

> "Țara românească și-a păstrat tradițiile străvechi de-a lungul secolelor."

<audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/eduardem/xtts-v2-romanian/resolve/main/samples/costel/sample_00.wav"></audio>

> "Ștefan cel Mare a construit mănăstiri și cetăți în întreaga Moldovă."

<audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/eduardem/xtts-v2-romanian/resolve/main/samples/costel/sample_01.wav"></audio>

### Mărioara (female, expressive storytelling) — 6.1% WER

> "Țara românească și-a păstrat tradițiile străvechi de-a lungul secolelor."

<audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/eduardem/xtts-v2-romanian/resolve/main/samples/marioara/sample_00.wav"></audio>

### Georgel (male, solemn delivery) — 1.8% WER

> "Țara românească și-a păstrat tradițiile străvechi de-a lungul secolelor."

<audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/eduardem/xtts-v2-romanian/resolve/main/samples/georgel/sample_00.wav"></audio>

### Lăcrămioara (female, clear broadcast style) — 7.2% WER

> "Țara românească și-a păstrat tradițiile străvechi de-a lungul secolelor."

<audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/eduardem/xtts-v2-romanian/resolve/main/samples/lacramioara/sample_00.wav"></audio>

### Dorel (male, conversational) — 14.5% WER

> "Țara românească și-a păstrat tradițiile străvechi de-a lungul secolelor."

<audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/eduardem/xtts-v2-romanian/resolve/main/samples/dorel/sample_00.wav"></audio>

## Key Innovation: Unicode Diacritics Normalization

Romanian uses **comma-below** diacritics (s-comma U+0219, t-comma U+021B), but many text sources contain visually identical **cedilla** variants (s-cedilla U+015F, t-cedilla U+0163) inherited from legacy encodings. These are different Unicode codepoints that map to different token embeddings.

This model solves the problem at two levels:

1. **Smart embedding initialization** -- new Romanian token embeddings were initialized from their closest existing donors (Turkish cedilla characters) rather than random weights, giving the model a meaningful starting point.
2. **Runtime normalization** -- all input text must be normalized to comma-below form before inference (see Quick Start below).

## Quick Start

### Installation

```bash
pip install TTS==0.22.0
```

> **Note**: TTS 0.22.0 requires patches for PyTorch 2.x compatibility and Romanian tokenizer support. See [setup_runpod.sh](https://codeberg.org/eduardm/romanian-tts-xtts-v2/src/branch/main/scripts/setup_runpod.sh) for the exact patches needed.

### Download Model

```bash
# Clone the model repo
git lfs install
git clone https://huggingface.co/eduardem/xtts-v2-romanian
cd xtts-v2-romanian
```

Or download individual files:
```python
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download

for fname in ["config.json", "model.pth", "dvae.pth", "mel_stats.pth", "vocab.json", "speakers_xtts.pth"]:
    hf_hub_download(repo_id="eduardem/xtts-v2-romanian", filename=fname, local_dir="xtts-v2-romanian")
```

### Basic Inference

```python
import torch
import torchaudio
from TTS.tts.configs.xtts_config import XttsConfig
from TTS.tts.models.xtts import Xtts

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# REQUIRED: Normalize cedilla -> comma-below before every inference
# Without this, diacritics will be silently mispronounced or skipped.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
CEDILLA_TO_COMMA = str.maketrans({
    "\u015f": "\u0219",  # ş -> ș  (lowercase s)
    "\u0163": "\u021b",  # ţ -> ț  (lowercase t)
    "\u015e": "\u0218",  # Ş -> Ș  (uppercase S)
    "\u0162": "\u021a",  # Ţ -> Ț  (uppercase T)
})

# Load model
config = XttsConfig()
config.load_json("xtts-v2-romanian/config.json")
model = Xtts.init_from_config(config)
model.load_checkpoint(config, checkpoint_dir="xtts-v2-romanian", use_deepspeed=False)
model.cuda()

# Prepare text -- always normalize!
text = "Bună ziua, mă numesc Alexandru și sunt din București."
text = text.translate(CEDILLA_TO_COMMA)

# Clone a voice from a ~6s reference clip
gpt_cond_latent, speaker_embedding = model.get_conditioning_latents(
    audio_path=["xtts-v2-romanian/reference_voices/costel.wav"]
)

# Generate speech
out = model.inference(
    text=text,
    language="ro",
    gpt_cond_latent=gpt_cond_latent,
    speaker_embedding=speaker_embedding,
    temperature=0.3,
    top_p=0.7,
    top_k=30,
    length_penalty=0.8,
    repetition_penalty=10.0,
)

torchaudio.save("output.wav", torch.tensor(out["wav"]).unsqueeze(0), 24000)
```

### Voice Cloning with Your Own Voice

You can clone any voice from a ~6-second WAV reference clip:

```python
# Use your own reference audio (WAV, ~6 seconds, clear speech)
gpt_cond_latent, speaker_embedding = model.get_conditioning_latents(
    audio_path=["my_voice.wav"]
)

out = model.inference(
    text="Aceasta este o propoziție de test în limba română.".translate(CEDILLA_TO_COMMA),
    language="ro",
    gpt_cond_latent=gpt_cond_latent,
    speaker_embedding=speaker_embedding,
)
```

### Inference Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `temperature` | 0.3 | Sampling temperature. Lower = more deterministic. |
| `top_p` | 0.7 | Nucleus sampling threshold. |
| `top_k` | 30 | Top-k sampling. |
| `length_penalty` | 0.8 | Values <1.0 discourage overly long output. |
| `repetition_penalty` | 10.0 | Penalizes repeated tokens. |

## Voices

Five voices are included with reference audio clips in the `reference_voices/` directory.

| Voice | Speaker ID | Description | WER |
|---|---|---|---|
| Costel | `speaker_male_literature` | Male, literary narration | 1.9% |
| Mărioara | `speaker_female_hp` | Female, expressive storytelling | 6.1% |
| Lăcrămioara | `speaker_female_adr` | Female, clear broadcast style | 7.2% |
| Georgel | `speaker_male_bible` | Male, solemn delivery | 1.8% |
| Dorel | `speaker_male_4` | Male, conversational | 14.5% |

WER is measured per-voice on 10 test sentences (5 diacritics-heavy + 5 common phrases) using Whisper large-v3. Lower is better.

## Training

### Dataset

[eduardem/romanian-speech-v1](https://huggingface.co/datasets/eduardem/romanian-speech-v1) -- approximately 62,000 clips totaling ~150 hours of Romanian speech from 5 speakers, sampled at 22,050 Hz.

### Infrastructure

- **GPU**: NVIDIA RTX 5000 Ada (32 GB) on RunPod
- **Training time**: ~42 hours (50 epochs, ~51 minutes per epoch)
- **Global steps**: 678,350
- **Final loss** (epoch 45): mel=2.72, text=0.025

### Two-Phase Training Strategy

**Phase 1 -- Embedding Warmup** (1 epoch)
- Freeze all GPT layers; train only `text_embedding` and `text_pos_embedding` (1.4% of parameters)
- Learning rate: 1e-4
- Purpose: bring the 6 new Romanian token embeddings (ă, â, î, ș, ț, `[ro]`) from random initialization to a meaningful representation before unfreezing the full model

**Phase 2 -- Full GPT Fine-Tune** (50 epochs)
- Unfreeze all GPT layers
- Learning rate: 5e-6
- Batch size: 4, gradient accumulation: 63 (effective batch size = 252)
- Optimizer: AdamW (betas=0.9, 0.96)
- `text_ce_weight=0.01` (auxiliary regularizer, not primary objective)
- `gpt_use_masking_gt_prompt_approach=True` (prevents reference audio parroting)

### Critical Training Parameters

These values are non-negotiable for XTTS-v2 fine-tuning:

- **Effective batch size >= 252** -- the official Coqui recipe minimum. Smaller batches cause mode collapse.
- **text_ce_weight = 0.01** -- increasing this breaks the mel/text loss balance and causes text-prediction shortcuts.
- **gpt_use_masking_gt_prompt_approach = True** -- without this, the model learns to copy the reference audio instead of conditioning on input text.

## Evaluation

WER progression during training, measured on held-out test sentences with Whisper large-v3:

| Checkpoint | Overall WER | Diacritics WER | Common WER |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 (warmup) | 144.9% | 146.3% | 143.6% |
| Epoch 5 | 18.3% | 15.9% | 20.7% |
| Epoch 10 | 7.7% | 7.9% | 7.5% |
| Epoch 15 | 6.6% | 7.0% | 6.2% |
| Epoch 20 | 4.7% | 6.0% | 3.4% |
| Epoch 25 | 9.1% | 11.0% | 7.2% |
| Epoch 30 | 7.3% | 6.9% | 7.8% |
| Epoch 35 | 11.5% | 10.7% | 12.2% |
| Epoch 40 | 7.3% | 3.8% | 10.9% |
| **Epoch 45** | **6.3%** | **5.9%** | **6.7%** |
| Epoch 50 | 7.9% | 7.6% | 8.3% |

Epoch 45 is selected as the release checkpoint. Epoch 50 shows WER regression (7.9%), suggesting early overfitting. Training loss decreases monotonically throughout, while WER fluctuates -- a common pattern in TTS where automatic metrics don't perfectly correlate with perceptual quality.

## Model Files

| File | Size | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `config.json` | 4 KB | XTTS-v2 configuration |
| `model.pth` | 2.1 GB | Fine-tuned model weights |
| `dvae.pth` | 211 MB | Discrete VAE for mel-spectrogram tokenization |
| `mel_stats.pth` | 1 KB | Mel-spectrogram normalization statistics |
| `vocab.json` | 270 KB | Extended vocabulary with Romanian diacritics + `[ro]` |
| `speakers_xtts.pth` | 8 MB | Speaker embedding defaults |
| `reference_voices/` | — | ~6s WAV clips for each of the 5 voices |

## Limitations

- **5 voices only** -- the model may not generalize well to Romanian accents or dialects not represented in the training data.
- **WER is Whisper-based** -- Whisper large-v3 is used as an automated metric; no human evaluation has been conducted. Whisper itself may have biases on Romanian text.
- **Library patches required** -- the TTS 0.22.0 library needs patches for PyTorch 2.x compatibility and Romanian tokenizer support. See `setup_runpod.sh` in the [Codeberg repo](https://codeberg.org/eduardm/romanian-tts-xtts-v2).
- **Cedilla normalization is mandatory** -- forgetting to normalize input text will silently degrade output quality for any word containing s or t with diacritics.

# 达妮娅音色 · GPT-SoVITS v2（粉丝向）

音色来自 **《鸣潮》（Wuthering Waves）角色「达妮娅」**。这是粉丝向的二次创作，**非官方**，与库洛游戏（Kuro Games）无关。

## 文件

| 文件 | 说明 |
|---|---|
| `dania_v2-e12.ckpt` | GPT 权重（第 12 轮） |
| `dania_v2_e10_s630.pth` | SoVITS 权重（第 10 轮 / step 630） |

## 用法

配合 GPT-SoVITS v2 使用：

```python
pipe.init_vits_weights("dania_v2_e10_s630.pth")
pipe.init_t2s_weights("dania_v2-e12.ckpt")
# 然后 pipe.run({... "ref_audio_path": <任意达妮娅参考音>, "prompt_text": ...})
```

参考音频与 prompt 文本需自行准备（本仓库不附带训练语料）。
